newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. wants changes in Iraqi-oil-for-food plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants changes in Iraqi-oil-for-food plan.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it wanted changes in the limited oil sales plan agreed by Iraq and the United Nations following President Saddam Hussein's sending of troops into the northern Kurdish provinces.
U.S. envoy Edward Gnehm told reporters that conditions in the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed between Iraq and the United Nations on May 20 had now changed and needed to be reopened.
"It's a matter of going back to the MOU and looking at it, he told reporters. "It was a designed programme and those conditions do not exist anymore."

The oil-for-food plan allows Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to purchase badly-needed food and medicine for its people, suffering under sanctions imposed when Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.

Diplomats said the entire programme was based on the fact that $240 million of the revenues were reserved for Kurdish areas in the north not under Baghdad's control. Detailed changes have not been discussed, but the issue is expected to be raised at an informal Security Council session later on Tuesday.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Sunday postponed implementation of the oil-for-food plan, expected later this month. He said he could not send U.N. staff to monitor it because he feared for their safety. Gnehm speculated the implementation now could take months.
